case_name: C. V. Govindappa and Others v State of Karnataka
facts: The appellant is challenging the judgment of the High Court of Karnataka convicting him for offences under Sections 302, 304 and 498-A I.P.C.
The appellant married Yashodhamma in September 1976.
On 26.1.1984 there was a quarrel between husband and wife which was noticed by the neighbors.
Even before that the appellant's wife had told the neighbours that her husband had poured kerosene oil on her and set fire.
The appellant went to the hospital later in the night and saw his wife in the ward.
On 27.1.1984 the statement of the appellant's wife was recorded by PW 27, P.S.I. Extension Police Station, Devangere.
The Court Session disbelieved the evidence adduced by the prosecution and accused.

Though the High Court refused to accept the credibility of the statement containing dying declaration escorted by PW 27 and also the entry in the Accident Register of the hospital containing the version given by the deceased, accepted the evidence of PWs 2, 13 and 14 and then factum of dying declaration made to them by the deceased.
Before us it is vehemently contended by the learned counsel for the appellant that there are several loopholes in the case of the prosecution which make it unworthy of acceptance.

It is further argued that the evidence of the doctor PW 6 who admitted the deceased in the hospital proved that she was not in a position to speak at all and she could not therefore have made any statement immediately prior to the admission in the hospital to PWs 12 to 14.
issues: The legal questions or points of law being debated
petitioner_arguments: There are several loopholes in the case of the prosecution which make it unworthy of acceptance.
The evidence of PWs 12 to 14 is of no value as there is no explanation for their not taking any steps to inform the police immediately.
There is no explanation for non-examination of the two persons who were sent by PW 12 to give message to the incident.

The doctor PW 6 who admitted the deceased in the hospital proved that she was not in a position to speak at all and she could not therefore have made any statement immediately prior to the admission in the hospital to PWs 12 to 14.
respondent_arguments: The evidence of PWs 2, 13 and 14 is quai natural and there is no reason whatever to reject the same.
There is no merit in this contention.

Even assuming that the deceased was not in a position to speak when she reached the hospital, it cannot be said by any stretch of imagination that she was not in a position to speak either in the auto rickshaw or before that.
court_reasoning: The conduct of the appellant soon after the incident is undoubtedly a circumstance to be taken into account for deciding the question whether the appellant was guilty.
Their neighbors have witnessed the incident, after the wife of the appellant came running out of the house and fell on the ground.
We do not find anything unnatural in the conduct of PWs 12 to 14.
The memo is in a prescribed form found in a book obviously kept by the hospital.
There is absolutely no substance in this contention.
holding: The High Court has found that the evidence of the aforesaid three witnesses is quai natural and there is no reason whatever to reject the same.
We are unable to accept any of the contentions urged by the appellant's learned counsel.

The evidence of PWs 12 to 14 has been accepted by the high court and in our opinion nothing has been placed on record to show that any of the three witness is motivated to speak against the appellant.
